# RustyNES v2.4.8 "Palimpsest"

**Read-modify-write, and a gate that cannot see its own subject.**

A palimpsest is a surface written over an earlier text, where the earlier writing is still there underneath. That is literally what a 6502 read-modify-write does to a memory location: it writes the old byte back before it writes the new one, so the address is written twice and the first write carries the value that was already there.

This release implements that group in SystemVerilog in the sibling repository — `ASL`, `LSR`, `ROL`, `ROR`, `INC`, `DEC`, across the accumulator form and four memory modes, 28 opcodes. Rung 1 now stands at **five ROMs, 1110 records**, matching the oracle on all seven CPU fields. `opgroup5` contributes 358 records and every construct in it is new; the four earlier ROMs are re-run unchanged at 147, 140, 286 and 179.

Written from public documentation only — the NESdev wiki's 6502 instruction, addressing-mode and cycle-time pages. No reference NES core was opened; none is present in the tree.

## The release is named for something this rung cannot verify

Hardware writes the **unmodified** byte back before writing the modified one. Two mutations, run from a verified-clean baseline, say plainly that the gate cannot see it:

| mutation | result |
|---|---|
| the dummy write is skipped entirely | **NOT CAUGHT** |
| the dummy write emits the modified value | **NOT CAUGHT** |

Neither changes a register, a flag, the final memory contents, or the cycle count — and `CpuBootTrace` carries exactly `pc`, `a`, `x`, `y`, `p`, `s` and `cycle`. An implementation performing one write instead of two is *identical* on every field this rung compares.

It is not a harmless difference on real hardware. That middle write lands on mapper registers and I/O, and writing twice to `$2007` or an MMC1 register is not the same as writing once. Verifying it needs the per-cycle bus comparison, which is **rung 2**.

The RTL implements the double write. The claim that it does rests on the code and on `docs/rung1-6502.md`, **not** on a green gate — and that is recorded rather than glossed, because a rung that quietly appeared to cover its own namesake would be precisely the failure this programme exists to catch.

The other eight mutations were caught.

## The mutation harness poisoned its own baseline

The script captured its pristine copy at *source* time and restored at the **start** of each mutation rather than the end. So the last mutant of a batch stayed on disk, and re-sourcing the script for the next batch captured **that** as the baseline.

Two mutations were therefore silently live in the working tree — "INC writes carry" and "RMW is one cycle short" — while every later result was measured against them, and both were reported CAUGHT for free. Worse, the gate's own first PASS had been against a stale binary. The sequence read as: implement, pass on the first try, mutate, all green. Every part of that was false.

What exposed it was a restore-and-reverify that **diverged after the restore**, on a source `diff -q` called identical to the baseline — which is only possible if the baseline is itself the mutant.

`tb/mutate.sh` replaces the ad-hoc script and fixes the class rather than the instance: the baseline is captured **once**, into a file the script refuses to overwrite; the baseline must **pass** the gate before any mutation runs, since a broken baseline reports every mutation as caught; there are **three** outcomes, because a mutant that does not compile is evidence about nothing; and a trap restores on exit, so an interrupt cannot leave a mutant behind.

This is the third distinct form of the same failure this project has recorded. The previous two were an interrupted run leaving its mutant on disk, and a restore leaving a stale build. This one is re-capture.

## A real gap the mutation pass found

"Zero-page indexed RMW uses a 16-bit add" came back **NOT CAUGHT**, because every zero-page-indexed access in the ROM stayed below `$FF` — where an 8-bit add and a 16-bit one agree on every byte. `$20 + $F5 → $0015` was added, with a sentinel at `$0115` that a straying access would disturb. Now caught.

## Design notes

**RMW is a flag on the existing addressing modes, not four new ones.** Four new `am_e` entries would have taken that enum from 14 values to 18 and overflowed its four bits — the exact defect v2.4.7 hit on `op_e`. The address computation is already correct for every mode; only the tail differs, and uniformly: read at the access cycle, dummy write at +1, real write at +2.

**Absolute-indexed RMW is seven cycles whether or not the index carries.** A read may take a fast path when the low-byte add does not carry; a read-modify-write never may. Both forms are in the ROM, and the difference between a correct implementation and a fast-pathed one is visible *only* in the cycle count — every register agrees.

**`INC` and `DEC` are the two members of the group that leave carry alone**, and the shifter holding its previous value is what implements that. The accumulator and memory forms share one shifter, so their results cannot disagree.

**With carry clear, `ROL` is indistinguishable from `ASL` and `ROR` from `LSR`.** The ROM runs the rotates with carry both set and clear, because an implementation that ignores the carry input passes every test that forgets to set it first.

## When the double write becomes verifiable

Rung 2, and specifically **v2.4.9** — folded in beside the undocumented opcodes rather than left to v2.5.0, because the bus half needs no new RTL and this release's own namesake is currently unverified.

The compare surface already exists on both sides: `Observable` is defined in the oracle's `checkpoint.rs` and the DUT's `tb/checkpoint.h` with a byte-identical wire encoding, both selftested, and the oracle already emits it. The CPU already exposes its whole bus. So the missing piece is a trace writer, not a new format.

That was tested rather than estimated, and the experiment paid immediately: wiring it produced **7 divergences across 793 cycles** on a program rung 1 scores 358/358. Two causes, needing different fixes — the testbench zeroes RAM the oracle seeds, so every dummy read of unwritten memory diverges; and there is a genuine per-cycle access difference on the absolute-indexed store's dummy-read cycle, where instruction boundaries still agree. Which is the plan's own justification for rung 2, arriving on first contact: *a 6502 can pass nestest with entirely wrong dummy reads.*

Two alignment facts, both of the family that has already bitten this programme once: the DUT emits the reset sequence while the oracle's per-cycle trace starts at cycle 8, so alignment is by cycle number and never by index; and the oracle's `Observable.pc` reads zero in all 793 records, so `pc` cannot be compared as-is.

**Interrupts stay at v2.5.0.** `cpu6502` has no `nmi_n`/`irq_n` pins and no `BRK`, so `nmi_line`, both IRQ samples and `put_cycle` will be inert at v2.4.9 — and the comparison must *declare* that it skips them, rather than silently comparing four constants against the oracle's real values.

## Verification

No crate under `rustynes-{cpu,ppu,apu,mappers,core}` changes, so **AccuracyCoin 141/141 (100.00%, RAM decoder) and nestest 0-diff hold by construction.**
